item.title: What Jensen Huang's Stunning Return Means for the AI Trade
item.ns0:encoded:
On Monday morning, Nvidia's board stunned the world and announced that it was reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO. Reportedly, President Trump pressed the board to bring back Huang, and his return kicked off a historic rally for the chip maker. (Nasdaq 100 futures went up so fast yesterday, they briefly halted trading.) All of this follows a weekend full of doom and gloom; the S&P 500 was entering correction territory last Friday, just days after Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. When we spoke with Alexander 'Alty' Altmann, global head of equities tactical strategies at Barclays, at the end of October, the AI trade was wobbling. Now, a month later, the AI trade seems, at least for now, ascendant, riding an epic rally that few saw coming. Today, we speak with Altmann about how Wall Street is making sense of Jensen's return, why structural issues around AI revenue and financing won't be fixed anytime soon, and if AI is really too big to fail.

Read more:
Stocks Jump Most Since April 2025 as Huang Is Back: Markets Wrap
US Blacklists Megaspeed, Targeting a Key Player in Nvidia Crisis

item.title: What a Town Full of Vibecoders Says About the Chinese Economy
item.ns0:encoded:
According to Stanford's AI Index, 84% of people surveyed in China say they are optimistic about AI. In the US, by contrast, 38% of those surveyed say they are optimistic. That's a big gulf in enthusiasm, and you can see it borne out in the stories you read. While in the US we hear about AI doomsday scenarios, in China, you'll hear about grandmas who are obsessed with using OpenClaw. Journalist Afra Wang has spent a lot of time in mainland China reporting from the country's AI hotbed — in a vibecoding-obsessed town outside of Hangzhou; at the for-profit schools where influencers are teaching everyday people how to use the technology; and the content studios that are pumping out AI microdramas. She understands, better than most, how AI is reshaping everyday life in China, and for today's episode, we talk to her about her reporting on AI in China and how the technology is actually diffusing into Chinese society.

item.title: How AI Is Forcing China to Reshape Industrial Policy
item.ns0:encoded:
Can Chinese tech companies help the country achieve technological self-reliance while keeping up in the AI arms race? On this episode, we speak with Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center and author of the High Capacity newsletter, about Beijing’s response to the global AI boom and the tensions between Chinese companies’ commercial ambitions and the government’s long-term plans. He explains how companies draw on shared expertise and supply chains to expand across industries including smartphones, robotics, EVs and semiconductors — and we also discuss Huawei’s efforts to compete with Nvidia and why technological success doesn’t necessarily translate into strong returns for stock investors in China.

Read more:
AI Threatens to Make China’s Jobs Slump Much Worse
China AI Biotech Firm Raises $200 Million in Oman-Backed Round

item.title: How an American AI Company Uses Chinese Open-Weight Models
item.ns0:encoded:
This week, we got news that the Trump administration is reportedly considering a requirement for US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models. Any effort to discourage US businesses from using Chinese open-source could be a big deal for both the AI industry and the market, where investors are still debating whether customers will ultimately be willing to pay for pricier homegrown frontier models versus cheaper alternatives. Everyone remembers last year's 'DeepSeek moment' for AI, when a Chinese company released a cheaper model that seemed nearly as good as cutting-edge US ones. So why do businesses actually use open-source? And what are the considerations that take into account in doing so? In this episode, we talk to Daniel Saedi, co-founder of Minerva, to better understand how an AI native company chooses its models. He breaks down how exactly his company mixes and matches models for specific use cases, the risk of abliterated models, and the issue of data sovereignty.

Read more:
India Startup Sells DeepSeek Access While Pursuing Sovereign AI
Anthropic Raises $107.3 Billion to Top SpaceX’s Record Debut

item.title: This Is The Problem With AI's Most Bullish Chart
item.ns0:encoded:
It has been a historic week for AI: the Anthropic IPO and the ongoing situation at Nvidia headline a pretty head-spinning time for the industry. Despite Nvidia's earnings outlook looking good, and despite the scale of the Anthropic IPO — it's oversubscribed, as you might know — there are so many open questions about the state of the industry right now. Financing the buildout has become increasingly complicated, and the Democrats who won races in the midterms know that data center opposition is a winning issue. Today's episode is a special two-parter that addresses some of these questions. First, we speak with Stanley Lee, the chief product officer at Liquid Compute, and he explains why Wall Street and Silicon Valley seem to be talking past each other, and what fragilities are emerging in the credit market for GPUs. All those charts that show rising GPU rental rates, Lee tells us, might not be as industry-bullish as they first appear. Then, we turn to Paul Kedrosky, a managing partner at SK Ventures, to discuss why “number goes up and to the right” does not necessarily prove the viability of the capex involved in the AI buildout, and also if Nvidia will remain the central bank for AI.

Read more:
Anthropic Said to Be Weighing IPO Price as High as $85 Per Share
Nvidia Sizes Up Arm CEO Haas in Search for Huang Successor

item.title: How GTA VI Became the Most Expensive Video Game Ever Made
item.ns0:encoded:
It took over a decade to make Grand Theft Auto VI. And when it's released on November 19, it will have likely already set at least one record: the most expensive video game ever made. In the years since the last GTA release, the video game industry has changed massively. Investors, once excited by the prospect of blockbuster video games, have pulled back, sales have stagnated, and the industry as a whole seems more precarious. Bloomberg News video game reporter Jason Schreier has been following Rockstar Games and its quest to release GTA VI for a long time. Ahead of the launch, we speak with him about why it took 13 years — and a budget that reportedly exceeded $1 billion — to get GTA VI across the finish line, and his impressions of the game having played it before almost anyone else on the planet.
